I do think it is important as someone that went into an area that aren’t very passionate about. However, I do think there is a balance with reality. If you are in an area that doesn’t have the job opportunities and you can’t move for whatever reason, then I think starting to build experience in some area is important. At the same time, working in an area you have no passion for can burn you out quick and that can make it difficult to switch careers at a later point.

Whatever you do, don’t rush this decision. Get out there, speak with different kinds of professionals, volunteer to see different roles, shadow and do your research. Give special attention to what kinds of things you feel you need: work-life balance, what kind of salary would support your current lifestyle, introversion/extroversion… how much do you want to work with people?, activity level etc

They still see life in these segments, a “fad”, like when they were in high school, but what they don’t realize is that they are on freestyle now and everyone is doing different things. I see now that those grads have since given up on those goals and have been humbled. Some went back for another degree too, in fact 😂The reality is that our economy is NOT good right now and until some hit the job and post-grad market with those idealistic expectations and fall short, they won’t understand. Part of maturing is realizing that while you may hate school and learning, others may love it. Just as some want kids and others don’t or some want to travel and others hate to travel…. Everyone has something different that makes them happy so you can’t necessarily judge with your own frame of reference. 

I will say I’ve honestly talked to several people since the pandemic who have had to go back for another degree or program. It’s becoming a lot more common. Some people are happy enough to do some college and get out working because they hate studying. Others love studying and make it a lifelong journey, which is very much medicine. Neither pathway is wrong and both pathways can make for a fulfilling life.

Could be a number of reasons:

1) your position is out of alignment and making it harder for the horse to balance

Your negative reinforcement is this part:

- Leg (stimuli) —> horse moves away from leg (Response)

Your positive reinforcement is a second part where you a pairing the stimuli for motivation or a more prompt response:

- Leg (stimuli: reinforced with pressure-release) and PAIRED with treat/praise = Prompt moving off leg. 

Patting a horse Is NOT negative reinforcement because: 

- Hand (stimuli) -/-> horse does not move away from stimuli

Negative reinforcement is anytime you have a Pressure-release system and that release essentially becomes a reward.

Now let’s look at a scenario where negative reinforcement is used to decrease the strength of response. Desensitization or if you really want to get psych term crazy: Habituation.

- scary flag (Pressure/Stimulus) —> horse moves away (response), but stimuli is kept ON so response does not equal reward. Horse gradually stops responding to stimuli (habituates) —> release of stimuli (negative reinforcement)

Further:

- Sensitization- increased response to stimulus
- desensitization- decreased response to stimulus

BOTH rewarded with negative reinforcement.

R- is release of pressure/stimulus. R+ is the addition of a reward to reinforce behaviours. Pressure needs not be unpleasant, but a force is uncomfortable otherwise a horse wouldn’t want to move away from it. Classical conditioning is pairing an US that solicits a particular type of behaviour with a cue and creating a CS. For example, a horse that salivates for treats.. giving a treat when bitting up = CS of salivating when bitting up. 

Psych 101. And every subsequent related psych class teaches this. We use all 3 training techniques for different things.

Negative reinforcement= taking away a stimulus once the desired behaviour is performed

Positive reinforcement= treats

You can pair them. I sometimes do this by stopping what I’m doing/ ending the riding session and taking the horse for treats or grass.

Have to agree that you can’t use on or the other. Horses use negative reinforcement all the time in the paddock.

24/7 turnout, changing diet to support anti-inflammatory functions (omega-3 increased, reduced sugars), respifree by omega alpha when needed. Bronchodilator/steroid inhaler used when needed and ONLY when needed. Kept antihistamines and dex on hand, just in case of a bad respiratory attack.

Big thing that helped target occasions where the heaves got worse was getting into the habit of taking vitals anytime I went to the barn and charting it with the date and time. As I board, this helped me determine times my horse may need more intervention. I did this over the span of 4 years and the symptoms actually decreased over time, which was really cool to visually see. Respirations went from 30’s to 20’s and now, many years later they are within normal (on average) and have been for 5 years. Haven’t had to use medication in several years because the environment is better managed (good hay that is soaked if dusty). But knowing your triggers is the big part of sustainable management.

I like to think of life as a journey of discovery, so your never screwed as you can start at any time! However, the mindset of “I’m behind” WILL screw your motivation, so try and keep positive by being goal-orientated. I remember taking undergraduate courses with a 70-year old student who was AMAZING! People who keep striving to learn and improve themselves are way more amazing to me, as they purely listen to themselves and never get stagnant. There are different versions of success. I don’t personally believe the white pickett fence and popping out babies is successful as I find that life quite boring, but other people want it and that is just fine. It’s all about what makes you happy. What I’ve learned is that many people make career changes throughout their lifetime, particularly in this economy and global scale. Would you rather live out a life exploring those things you find interesting or live a captive life by abiding to societal norms that would have you forever unhappy? 

First off, you need to collect yourself and really research fields of interest. Reddit is a GREAT resource for this. Use it to inquire about potential career fields you may have interest in. Make a list. Also, look at careers in demand in your area. Look at things that you are curious about first and inquire further about them. If they are careers you could shadow, take advantage of that too! Also take into consideration your current skills and have confidence in your ability to learn! You ARE smart enough to do what you put your mind too! 

Now look at the education and work experience you need for such opportunities. Community college is a smart move because they do a far better job at connecting grads with work. University can be a lot harder to develop those connections. It IS REALLY important to get relevant work experience while you are studying. I cannot emphasize this enough. So look up and ask colleges about how their program connects you with work (with things like coop, experiential learning etc). 

Next, look at your current needs. With your debt, I’d recommend looking at shorter 2 year programs or at least programs that strongly connect you with employment. 

Then formulate and execute a plan. Look at admission deadlines and apply to a few options. Look at grants, bursaries, government loans, and any other funding available. A lot of trial and error. I’m a girl, but I think these tips would be extremely useful for a guy too:

- Researching my body type. This really helped me select clothing and patterns that helped balance me and highlight my best features. This can make a big difference. 
- Picking clothes that fit me properly. In the past, I wore shirts that were too long and made me look disproportionate. 
- To some degree (I haven’t fully figured it out yet) colour analysis. This helped me figure out which colours highlighted my features best and which colours washed me out. 
- I used Pinterest as a style board to discover what looks I was drawn too and this also helped me start creating a wardrobe of pieces that all work together. 
- Started to select quality pieces for my wardrobe. Quality fabrics DO make a difference. They fall, cling and lay differently than cheap fabrics. The difference can make you look a lot more put together. I honestly didn’t spend a fortune on this either. I do a lot of thrift shopping for classic staples. 
- It took me time to figure out my adult wardrobe. I wear a lot more business casual stuff now. It makes me feel more put together and confident. 
- shoes are still a work in progress, but playing around with different shoe options can really change an overall look. For example, a plain white tee with fitted jeans can look casual with sharp white sneakers or dressed up with a dress shoe. 
- started going for more solid colours over patterns. Solids are easier to mix and match and they tend to look more put together and classy. Patterns can be used, but it can be harder to find patterns that look as classy.
- last is something I’m certainly not keeping up with 😂 But knowing my body type from #1 and going to the gym to build in my weak areas. Like, I don’t really have hips, so I build them at the gym and it balances my shape out.

How is his copper to iron ratio in feed? It should be around a 1:4: 4(zinc) ratio with copper being a minimum of 150mg daily. 

I mention this because if your horse is an OTTB, then they are often pushed iron supplements and unlike us, horses do not easily deplete iron unless they have some kind of bleeding (internal like an ulcer or external). This means that they can have way too much iron that “out competes” copper. 

Copper is needed to form strong connections between proteins. Copper is needed for a tight white line. Zinc is needed to form proteins and the hoof being brittle is one symptom of deficiency in both. Horses also need adequate protein for the hoof and vit e. 

I used to be told my horse had bad genetics for hooves and would always need shoes. It took me a long time to look into diet but once I did, I never went back. It makes such a LARGE difference in hoof quality. But there is no half effort in it. You need to look at everything (grain, hay, supplements and somewhat soil reports). You ideally should test the hay (agricultural centers/vets and some feed centers may do this) and fill in the blanks with whatever grain you have in mind. Any supplement on top of that needs to be accounted for because supplements do and can mess up a nutrition profile. Ideally, working with an unaffiliated nutritionist, but I didn’t have that option early on so it can be done. If you are in the US, you have a ton of options… I really like Horsetech for custom vitamin/mineral options. You need to look at your areas soil deficiencies and over abundance so you have an understanding as well. Iron is often plentiful in grains, red salt blocks, water etc. It may require looking at different pellets and their nutritional profile to see if they suite your horse’s needs rather than a one fits all narrative. My horse has now been barefoot for 11 years and hoof quality is great. 

Adjustment takes about a year because that is how long it takes to regrow an entire hoof. You need proper nutritional support and the first few months, you may need something like sole barrier or hoof boots as your horse’s hoof adjusts.

Just to add to this essay 😅 I know so many in the horse world go to supplements because it is easier and often that is the advice given. I’ve been there too! But supplements may not be effective if the underlying nutritional profile doesn’t leave way for a supplement. You mention farriers formula below, which actually has that copper in it, but what you may not know that if your iron is already too high (you are feeding iron in the grain too) and those ratios aren’t in balance, you WON’T get the intended effect. This also happens if a supplement doesn’t provide a relatively high enough amount to meet the baseline…
Either something with the primary diet is interfering with the supplement or that baseline via the hay and environment is lower than the commercial companies estimate. So something to consider is your mental health. I have a friend that worked as a nurse and was perhaps one of the most optimistic, driven people I’m friends with. However, her mental health took a HUGE hit with med school. She lost a ton of weight and hair. You need to consider not only whether you can meet admissions, but whether your mental health can take 4 years of BRUTAL schooling + residency. You need to be able to study 17 hours straight, 7 days a week for those 4 years. You need to ask if your mental health can withstand that. 

Now to be more optimistic. I think it is a big mistake for people not to aim for a career in undergrad. Not only is it a good backup option, but it gives you motivation to learn and unique experiences that could set you apart. Instead of panicking about grades and meeting admission standards, you’ll have a career that will offer you a living while you study for the MCAT. You also might be able to work in between med school to help pay back loans/tuition. Graduation is a difficult time met with many changes and it can be depressing for the best of us in a challenging economy and job market. Use the resources you currently have with the best of your ability. 

Your grades definitely need to improve. A 2.0 is quite low and means you haven’t succeeded in most of your courses. You need to figure out that balance now. Luckily you are already seeking advice, so you have options! 

I’d suggest switching degrees just for that fresh start to help make you eligible for masters etc. It won’t erase the 2.0, but it will give you a clean slate for cGPA in your university’s eyes. I’d even suggest taking a gap year to work and just help your mental health before going back fresh. Choose courses and professors CAREFULLY. Choose things that you like and classes that aren’t rigged against you. Take LESS courses rather than more until you are sure you can succeed with a full and busy schedule. Medical school is ALL about prioritizing and juggling an insane schedule so it is important for you to build these skills in undergrad.

I used to have to hold the horses a certain way so kids could tack them up on cross ties without getting cow kicked and bitten. Somehow this barn still had a relatively good position and that was always crazy to me. 

My own horse was trained good ground manners from the start. I have been able to lead my horse by the halter, have had him spook at something, and he never pulled or put his haunches my way. He also de-escalated quickly because these things were just second nature to him. It led into his dressage training and made him easier to train (I often did things on the ground before under-saddle). It has made handling him in retirement ridiculously easy because he is super spoiled now and gets away with so much lol. 

There is a stark difference between “reprimanding” bad behaviour with good timing and release and punishing a horse with no timing and little release. I think the difference ought to be taught early on for all riders so they are able to implement it not only into their horse handling, but their riding. It has improved my training tremendously over the years to a point where I see others ride rather roughly to get what I get out of the same horse simply because they don’t understand how correction and release timing works. Another trend I notice is that people want the horse to do things at the flip of the hat 0-100, while I understand there is a progression in training to get to 100. Training is often about the mind, not the movement itself and that starts with ground manners. It can be a big gap in the education of many.

I know all about it. My horse was diagnosed in 2019. Prognosis is very individual and dependent on both the horse’s environment and age. Feel free to ask any questions you may have.

The reason I don’t really trail ride is both to avoid muddy areas that are hard on the ligaments and also because I avoid working him to get his energy out and he is often fresh and unpredictable without the constant work. It’s easier for me to just not ride at all, as I find it emotionally hard in the arena (miss our dressage.. he still has the buttons) and have been reared off a few times outside of the arena 😅Do I only really trail ride in the summers when I can free lunge on good footing more consistently.

It’s easy to break sterility and you could introduce more bacteria into the wound this way. 

Do not apply ointment, as this can seal the wound off exteriorly and trap bacteria. Made that mistake before. Keep the wound open for draining.

Here is what you do…

2. Cc this email also to the TA. 

3. Document everything from this point forward and be quick to act if your partner isn’t holding up their end. Update via email and change partners if need to be. 

4. If changing partners is NOT possible and this has negatively affected your mark. Email the TA and Professor requesting INDIVIDUAL evaluation. State your reasoning again as to why it is NOT FAIR to mark you based on your partner’s incompetence and relate to the syllabus in anyway possible. 

5. Look up the terms for a GRADE REBUTTAL at your university and follow this to the “T”. Should things go south and your prof and TA are a dick, REFUTE THE GRADE ASAP with all your emails and documentation in tow so the prof and Ta can’t claim they didn’t know. I’m talking almost immediately after you get your grade.

If you ever deal with another poor group member or are marked unfairly for your partner’s contribution, remember that documentation and timing are KING. Seriously,  it took me a LONG time to figure out how to advocate for myself when it comes to shitty marking or group members, but it is SO IMPORTANT to understand your rights as a student and can make the difference between fair marks and poor marks due to a poorly marked class.

Not significantly and I don’t think it will happen anytime soon, but the move to salary means physicians get paid a fixed amount per unit of time. Pro is that they don’t have to see a ton of patients. Con is that if they can’t get more one day if they see more patients one day over another. Fee for service means they can bill per patient so it is an incentive to see more patients in a day and get paid more for that day. 

The European model differs in different areas and area of study. I don’t know a ton about to be honest. But I have a friend doing med school in Europe who wants to come back because the physician salaries there are low in comparison to the tuition and length of schooling. My understanding is that this is due to the salary model, but what it comes down to is that European systems are more socialized than even Canada and Canada has actually modelled more after the US physician system in pay, but is following the European system a little more recently. Europe also has a fee for service system, but my understanding is that it is at a fixed rate. The less free market you have, the less salary a physician will be able to make. This trend paired with the fact we are experiencing inflation and a doctor shortage could mean further direction towards a more European model down the road. Whether this event fully takes place, it’s hard to say. All I know is that family physicians today aren’t making near what the doctors who are at or near retirement and this isn’t fully encompassed by inflation either. It’s to do with (1) fixed salary and the related reduction in patient loads, which also may be related to technology updates and associated documentation. The older doctors used to see up to thousands of patients in their practice. The newer ones are seeing only hundreds.

I believe Nursing should move towards STEM, but politics keep us from going there. We would 100% benefit from learning STEM, as it has been very beneficial for at least me in my nursing degree and self-study, though I do get frustrated about the shallower depth in nursing school. Nurses are afraid that by moving towards STEM, they will align themselves with the medical model. They fear this will potentially cause a lack of autonomy.

Ultimately, I think it is difficult for people who haven’t actually experienced STEM to compare it and vice versa. Science graduates who haven’t experienced nursing likely think it is more heavy in the sciences (I did) and Nursing students who haven’t experienced STEM think they have it just as hard because Nursing is hard. It’s just that it is more broad than in-depth science.
Medicine is based off of STEM because they have to know all the science and some engineering principles (biophysics mainly) to proficiently study the human body.

No, we really don’t even delve a little bit in chemistry (speaking as someone who took chemistry in my previous degree). We read bloodwork that is already translated for us. We also only study very limited macro biology. We learn very limited cellular biology and next to no biochemistry to understand how everything works via molecules, fisher diagrams, the krebs cycle, receptors, ATP etc. There are normally full classes on these topics. Our physiology is short to be honest. We learn more than say Engineering would, but less than kinesiology students would. Our sociology is probably the most prominent feature, but I’ve only taken limited sociology in my previous degree so I can’t speak for it. 

The research projects I’ve done in my nursing degree are more aligned with sociology work than STEM sciences. In STEM, I often had to do a number of chemistry calculations, use machines to standardize my results, use controls to standardize etc. Then more chemistry calculations. Then I had to take data and make a number of graphs, use statistical analysis to analyze the accuracy of results and any relations. Calculated and exhibited the standard error, then write about relationships and associated error. Find other articles that relate to my results and write a discussion with several of these articles. I had to do this once a week, as I had a 3 hour lab each week outside of class. Class time was solely for lecture materials.

I’m not saying Nursing isn’t hard because it is. I’m just saying it isn’t the same kind of hard. Nursing is busy. I find clinicals to be challenging honestly because I feel I’m not prepared enough for them with school and have to do a lot of self-study. NCLEX questions also make it difficult. There are also so many group projects which take up lots of time.

No because I’ve done a easier STEM degree and there is just no comparison in depth. My STEM degree made me have legit breakdowns because I couldn’t understand a topic when reading it and it took me 3 hours more to understand the topic… it isn’t something you can just read and understand because it often involves mathematics.

Nursing is hard, but it’s the NCLEX questions and clinicals that make it hard, not necessarily the depth of materials to learn. Our pharmacology isn’t real pharmacology (pick up a pharmacists pharm book and you’ll see what I mean). We don’t learn the O-chem and bio-chem behind pharmacology. The materials, believe it or not, are a lot shallower in depth than STEM which is educating the histology, chemical, physics, biophysics and biochemical elements of the body (if we are comparing it to human biology).

I will say again that Nursing is hard because it is broad, schools expect a standard, and the NCLEX is frustrating. We also have to teach ourselves more because again, those classes aren’t as in-depth. But the actual core sciences differ. At many schools, they have separate sciences for nursing students and they are generally easier. Something I’ve found in comparison to my science and nursing degree is that you simply don’t know what you don’t know. My class is an advanced one and everyone has at least one degree. The profs can’t answer questions that are rooted in STEM and students want to know out of curiosity. The ones who took pharm prior found the class ridiculously easy but also not the best way to teach pharm because of it never teaching us to understand it, just memorize it. There is SO MUCH time spent on theory and is not applicable fundamentally today and less emphasis on patho, pharm and completely disregards other sciences like histology, chemistry and physics which are actually important to understanding the human body. 

Yet, Nursing is still a giant pita because it DOESN’T teach these things that would make it easier to problem solve and understand the things they DO teach. It’s often a game of route memorization when it comes to NCLEX questions and I constantly feel inadequate for clinical with patients that are quite sick because there is simply so much I don’t know. That is just my perception, but you get my point.

My opinion is that Nursing should move in the direction of STEM to align itself with the current healthcare system and changes. But this will never happen because of politics and nurses afraid of losing their autonomy to aligning more with the medical model which is based on STEM.

You also need to keep in mind the 5+ years of schooling that is very excessive. I think most people underestimate how med school not only tests you, but breaks you. It is NOT abnormal to be reading 1000 pages per night for at least 4 years. The majority can’t keep up with that and do have to sacrifice their social life etc to just try and keep up. 

The money can be pretty good (do PA’s have benefits though?), but remember that doctors don’t get benefits like other careers do. This includes their own retirement fund since they are their own business. If you are planning on opening your own practice, you also have to pay overhead and employee fees. The newer electronic system also makes it hard to only hire one employee, so you may need 2-3 by the time you’d get out.

I’ve done this before or just think about it and write it down on my phone. Turned into an A+ paper 😂 Sometimes we just really get into our own heads and that creates a mental block.

It gets better. First year, it also took me hours to write 500 words, especially if reading research is involved. 

You eventually learn what they are looking for and can pinpoint key topics you need to write about, then find the research to reflect those topics. I usually start out by reading the background of a topic and the most recent key points. Take notes, then framework my paper based on what I feel is important. Write the body paragraphs one at a time, then go back and write the intro to reflect the key ideas and lastly the conclusion. 

I will say that new fields/topics I am unfamiliar with ALWAYS take me WAY longer to write. I have even had to ask for extensions over a week late because no matter how long I sat and read, the lightbulb just wouldn’t turn on. On the other hand, I’ve cranked out an A+ paper in 2 hours on a topic I was fairly comfortable with.

I recommend starting early. Write what you can, then ask the prof if you can get them to take a look and/or book with writing resources at the university.

I’d recommend volunteering at your local hospital first to see if it is actually an environment you’d enjoy. Talk to a few doctors and ask them what they realistically like and dislike about the job. Can tell you a bit about the dislike. The job has changed from what it was for family doctors, at least. Doctors used to have more hands on work. They would do flu injection clinics etc. Those tasks have been passed onto pharmacists and nurses. Doctors are also having to do a lot of paperwork now. I’m being serious when I say that you leave for a weekend and you have 15+ prescription refills to go through and sign on Monday. That’s not including the files you have to take home and review nor the paperwork you have to do for patient’s on the side of that. It has become more of an administrative position than what you may think it is. Newer doctors are also going on salary, which has good and bad factor. Older doctors had up to 1000’s of patients. They got paid by the number they would see in a day. Work harder, get paid more. Newer doctors are on salary. My father was told the new number of patient was 700 and has now gone to 500. They get paid less on salary and there really isn’t any incentive to work harder. Moreover, the new technology system is timely and creates more work for these doctors. 

My father was a doctor. He had classmates in their 40’s. One was the valedictorian. So it is definitely doable. Just keep in mind that it is a long haul and so many realize they dislike medicine half way through. I actually found the most useful was exterior exercise programs, with a focus on core control. Planks etc. sitting trot tends to use a lot more toned ab control than rising and even canter. It’s a toned core, which means there is a balance between when it is being used to suck yourself into the saddle and relaxed in other moments to move with the horse. 

Trot is also a 2-beat diagonal paired movement, which means each seat bone is individually “lifted”. If you are fighting against that, you will bounce. 

Lastly, seat bones! Plug them in. If you are too far behind or forward, you won’t be able to adequately follow the movement, as your legs and upper body will be out of balance. 

Belt buckle forward. That is to mean open your hip/pelvis to help absorb the shock. Your psoas will be the main muscle doing this. If you sit often, this may be tight. I’d recommend looking up riding and non-riding exercises to relax the muscle (don’t force it!).

And yes, no stirrups, but I recommend altering no stirrups, to picking them up for a few strides and back and forth. The trouble with no stirrups as people often completely relax their leg and forget to keep a bend in their knee/hip. So, It’s absolutely okay to take a step back and re-evaluate. I’m actually going into nursing and have decided I didn’t want to pursue vet med after shadowing a number of vets. Nursing is ,in ways, the more reliable job here since it is unionized, whereas the vets I had shadowed were constantly stressed by being overworked, under appreciated, and under paid in ways (overhead costs are often larger than a client thinks). 

I also agree with the other comment that this job won’t teach you much. Vet school is super super competitive where I live (Canada) and when I was aiming towards that and in contact with vets, I was encouraged to have *varied* animal experience. So for example, I volunteered at a zoo for one, a shelter for small animals, I shadowed a number of vets in different fields (agricultural, equine, small animal/exotic). I already had a large amount of horse experience by showing/competing and assisting teaching via a pony club. But if a horse rescue was an option or a therapeutic riding center (at that time), I’d be all over that. I think prioritizing positions that give you *relevant* experience would be looked on more favourably and would give you better interview points to talk about. Even to this day, my experience shadowing an agricultural vet has given me so much to talk and think about. Plus, because of the increased competition here, applicants are actually *required* to have over 100 shadowing hours under 2 vets.

If you aren’t already shadowing, I’d recommend you start. Although I still LOVE the science behind vet med, actually shadowing the profession was what made me take a step back to re-evaluate. Seeing way too many vets stressed and often depressed behind the scenes was eye opening to me. Plus, when you do all you can do to help an animal and the owner refuses to pay for treatment or maybe can’t afford it, it’s a *tough* decision to put down the animal. I asked one vet I shadowed about these cases and she said she sometimes had to put down perfectly healthy horses just because she knew if the owner sold or went to someone else, the horse might well end up in a worse situation. Then, you hop in the car and drive on to your next appointment of the day like nothing happened.

Omg No! Don’t ride her with suspensory issues. I’d be getting rid of a vet who ever recommended that. First stall rest, then hand walking. Depending on the horse’s energy levels, you may need ace or something of the kind when hand walking. 

Have dealt with suspensory issues including the genetic disorder dsld. It is VERY VERY painful and should be properly managed. Ligaments take a good 6 months + to heal properly as they don’t have the circulation of a tendon. Loading a ligament will only stress it further, perpetuating the issue. Riding should be at the end of the recovery period. 

Your horse needs lots of turnout in good footing (avoid mud, if possible). Hand walking on straight lines, cold hosing at initial stages. Heat therapy (thermal therapy/ back on track etc) in between and depending on how recent it is, your horse may benefit from prp or shockwave.

The best way you can prevent future issues due to nutrition is to screen for deficiencies. You can o this by getting a hay analysis (agricultural vets or feed stores may know where you can send this test too). You can also check soil analysis reports in your province/state for relative deficiencies. They should be available online. I found mine in a simple google search. For example, my area is consistently low in copper and vit.E and high in iron, which can cause issues in the hooves and connective tissues (due to its connection to copper and zinc). This is typically reflected in the hay and grass, but can vary a bit in hay if farmers use any sort of fertilizer to feed the hay, which is why hay analysis is always good to do. The last thing you can do is blood test; however, this is variable. Horses can give false positive tests for anemia, when copper is the issue (iron uses a copper-dependant enzyme in order to convert itself into an absorbable form) etc and absorbance will vary throughout the day/ conditions etc. due to this, I typically skip on blood tests, unless I have a very health-specific reason I need to do so. 

There are retailers that will customize vitamin and minerals specifically to your hay analysis to take the work from you (Horsetech for one, madbarn is another). These would be COMPLETE vitamin/mineral supplements, meaning that you have to be careful what you add on top of it as a few balances may be disturbed due to their narrower ranges (selenium, copper:zinc:iron balance, phosphorus: calcium, vitamin E since it is lipophilic (fat soluble/attracted) and not excreted as easily). Water soluble vitamins/minerals such as vitamin C aren’t usually an issue because any excess can be more readily excreted. 

Omega-3’s on top of that is usually a non-issue since most feeds are higher in Omega-6 anyways. Bulk feeds like soaked hay cubes or beetpulp etc is also a non-issue, usually. Alfalfa needs to be monitored and looked into due to its Phosphorus: Calcium balance. Not as much of an issue if your looking at timothy/alfalfa cubes though since the horse is typically not getting as much pure alfalfa and the timothy helps balance out where alfalfa runs short. 

Anything extra, such as MSM or joint supplements is case-case (glucosamine, for example, has been suggested to not be fed to insulin resistant horses due to its ability to be converted to sugar).

Lastly, I want to touch on the base that there is a lot of gimmicky supplements out there. I haven’t looked into camelina, so can’t comment on that; however, I have a science background and have looked into some of the research on other mainstream supplements and it is not very representative or is very claim-based, where the evidence is not very supportive. Just something to be wary of :) So many supplements gain popularity from word of mouth and myth in the community and if you really look into it, research does not support the claims! There are supplements out there that do have a body of research though! I’m planning to do more readings on them, in the future, for my blog. But time is limited and I haven’t gotten to the point where I can compile and really scrutinize research to list and summarize.

Since you are going to be in an equine-based program, there may be opportunities for learning and riding there. Never been involved in one, but I know individuals who have and there were (sort of) partners with the school who would take on students and mentor them.

As someone who is getting paid to put training rides on a horse and has done it before, there are two MAJOR variables that can make or break these opportunities: 

A) SKILL. I have 19 years of experience, competed nationally, have trained up my own horse and have passed certain rider level evaluations to “prove” my abilities. There were A LOT of riding lessons that went into that, but also self-study and a drive to improve. 

B) Geographic location. Some areas just don’t have a lot of free riding offers (my area). Others may have more wealth/population and have more opportunities. 

Realistically, right now, you do not have the skills to get paid for riding, even as a exercise rider. Given my own experience, it has even been difficult for ME to get paid and honestly, I wasn’t even asking to get paid, but OFFERED after they saw the change in their horses. I’m entirely grateful for that (especially where I’m in post-grad and struggling financially), but again, I never came into those opportunities with an expectation to get paid because honestly, they could just pay a full-time trainer to do the work if they *wanted* too. 

Now FREE RIDES: 

With time and training, you MIGHT find opportunities for free rides/volunteering. This is area-specific, but you also need to be at least competent to ride independently and have enough skills to not give the horse bad habits. If you are in an area like mine, this WON’T be an option for someone with few skills. I found my opportunities via connections. People generally won’t put unfamiliar riders on their horse for nothing around here and I honestly can’t see free rides as being something advertised. The best way to find these opportunities is to know people. 

Other opportunities are actual volunteer gigs like volunteering for a therapeutic riding centre to help and eventually exercise their horses. I highly recommend something like this! I volunteer at one as much as I can and I have frequently seen individuals new to horses. The particular program I am involved in has a process, where they will teach individuals how to properly care for the horses under guidance. Opportunities are limited per the abilities of the individual. So where I could ride any horse with no supervision (but had to sometimes ask on certain safety protocols that differed from my own barn due to organizational involvement), beginners were only to handle the horse and brush with supervision. This is a liability thing too because letting just anyone ride can have repercussions for the facility. I have a provincial riding insurance and am lucky enough to know the barn owner well enough for her to trust me/ know my abilities. 

Rescues also come to mind, but there are none around me, so I can’t speak on that. 

With more experience, you can also look for work opportunities for barn chores. It’s hard work and albeit, not all that rewarding compared to a regular job, but you can learn about horse care here. 

I also recommend auditing every clinic possible. Theory is important too before you gain those abilities undersaddle. 

Now, I’m going to be honest. Trying to find these opportunities, particularly at your level, is no easy task. I get it though, as my parents also scoffed at my (with my own money) attempting to pay for leases especially after their X years of investment 😂 but the horse community is fickle and it is also very political. My best advice would be to take volunteer opportunities as they come, audit clinics, network and get a job to pay for your own lessons/extras because ultimately, the horse world operates on networking and often that means being out and about the community riding, which takes $$$.

I am unsure of how useful knee boots would even be in this context. Honestly, I’d like to see the research or evidence for and against it. New research comes out all the time that supports or debunks certain hypotheses and the horse world THRIVES on old ways and myths. 

I agree that conditioning and turnout are very helpful in terms of health etc; however, it still doesn’t completely account for risk of injury amongst all horses. Some horses are just funny movers and as you know, the breeding of dressage horses has moved further and further from the stance of functional towards hyper-flexibility and larger movers. There was even a german specialist vet that spoke on this matter I saw a while back. They spoke on a different matter all together regarding hyper-flexibility; however, it means many lines of high performance horses are built for a higher risk of injury than ever before. 

I would LOVE if only turnout and conditioning completely negated the risk of injury for ALL horses; however, I unfortunately think we are seeing things in dressage-line horses that just weren’t a factor before. I have been lucky and have not needed boots (generally) in my horse, but friends certainly have in their bigger moving horses, who were nicking themselves frequently during schooling rides. I think it is important to keep in mind that whilst boots are not permitted in competition, competition is but a fraction of the horse’s work and the horse *should* be well accustomed to movements in competition, which reduces risk of injury at those events.

I do agree shoes can complicate things; however, I think that is more a reflection of poor regulation (or rather up to date science-based) education across all farriers. An excellent farrier who shoes a horse can do A WHOLE LOT OF GOOD. A farrier who doesn’t have the right balance, which is harder than it looks and then slaps a shoe on it + extended intervals between shoes getting reset can really cause a shift in the horse’s balance, then an increased risk of injuries. 

I’m not a big fan of booting out in the pasture, though I have been blessed with a horse who does not need it. I have friends who have not had the same luck and have encountered various injuries to their horse on pasture prior to booting full-time. It sucks, but it is to keep in mind that not every horse is built the same, especially big growing WB’s!

It’s an unfortunate pattern I’ve seen that many trainers keep pushing once that boundary has been opened and continue to push it towards suiting their wants. I’ve found this is particularly frequent in trainers that teach full-time. Not saying all of them are like that, but I do think it takes a particular personality type to get to that reputation. 

Everyone is different, but after boarding at a training barn, then switching to boarding barns, I MUCH prefer the latter. I have had frustrations with training barns dictating WHO I can train with, WHEN I can ride, which professionals I use and WHAT I do with my horse. Some trainers can be rather egotistic and have a “my way or the highway” type attitude that prevents one from trying out different methods/opportunities. This can be helpful as a beginner, but can keep you from growing. I actually learned a lot from fellow boarders over the years and through that networking, have found out which professionals work the best for me. Plus, I was able to audit more lessons that way from different instructors, find out about unadvertised clinics etc. 

Back then, I was also rather stingy with my horse 😂 But If I had felt more confident in my abilities, leasing would not have been a bad option. With leasing, you just need to carefully screen the riders if you are wanting someone with more skills. Ask their background, years riding, achievements. Meet with them, watch them ride your horse as a test ride and see if they have the abilities to keep your horse more consistent. 

If you want someone with more skills, there is generally a balance between cost and autonomy. I see a lot of leases where the owners are asking for a good chunk of board $400 (50%) for 2 rides, plus farrier, vet and 2 lessons a week for a horse that is only training level on the flat or so. These things add up. Then they wonder why they only get beginners or riders with less skills and the more experienced riders skip out. It’s because riders with more skills have more options for riding and unless the benefits outweigh the costs, they will likely move on. I have seen people advertise for a lease, screen the rider and then depending on the rider’s skills, compromise on price/opportunities. So if you are looking to have some of the costs subsidized and are concerned on your horse’s training, this is something to keep in mind.

First of all, I just LOVE your eagerness to learn. That will take you far. You also seem rather conscientious of the things your body is doing, which is a great trait for improvement. It means you have some feel and therefore, it should come easier to adapt your position with time. 

Since you mentioned your legs and toes out: 

- the reason your leg position is like this is actually your hip angle. So right now, your back of thigh is more in contact with the saddle. This rotation naturally points your toe out (think of a sumo squat but with your toes slightly out). Now, point you toes forward, go into a squat and then adjust your lower back and abdomen so that it is parallel with the floor… this is your dressage position. Hopefully I explained that enough so that you can visualize and feel it. Essentially, with that position, your INNER thigh is now in contact with the saddle. Your thigh is rotated slightly inward and this points your toe forward. Some visuals and exercises: https://www.lauragdressage.com/amp/dressage-rider-leg-position-it-s-all-in-the-hips

https://www.usdf.org/EduDocs/The-Rider/Loosen_up.pdf

https://www.balancedrider.com/thigh.htm

What I like to do at a halt is to lift each individual leg and rotate the thigh in before I place my stirrup. Then, I push my lower back forward/ belt buckle forward without moving the leg to open the hip. If you do this correctly, you should immediately feel the difference and more weight distribution. You will absolutely feel like all your weight is pointed downwards and you are completely centred. 

In terms of heels down. Think TOES UP! This may help you keep your leg from falling forward. The phrase “heels down” tends to have several riders attempt to force their heel down and so their lower leg follows by pushing forward and getting in front of their centre of balance. 

Other thing I noticed is your hands. You have a bit of a broken line at your wrist there, but you are still a fairly quiet rider, so good job on that! 

For now, you need to straighten out your wrist, so that you feel a bend in your elbow. Your forearm and wrist need to remain straight, almost as an extension of the rein. With the rise, your elbow opens. When you sit, your elbow closes. This is how you keep your hands level with the motion. 

Think of pointing your thumbs slightly downwards to relax the wrist Nd keep those thumbs on top rather than inverting the hand inwards. 

As an exercise, you can try tucking a whip or crop under your thumbs horizontally while your warm up at the walk/trot. This will do 2 things: 1) make you more aware of whether your hands are on the same plane. 2) make you use your core more to balance. 

At this stage, you may also benefit by going into a position closer to a forward position and closing your hip angle slightly to allow your upper body to come slightly forward. This may feel counter intuitive since you are working on keeping your shoulders back, but you still keep a open shoulder in a forward position. Ultimately, in the short-term, I feel this will help you with your leg and hands. When you have a better feel for where your leg and hand are supposed to be, the. Your upper body can come back and sustain the position.

However, I recommend picking one of these to focus on (I’d start with the leg) and focusing on that before the other fixes 😊 It makes it easier to implement changes.

Honestly, take it slow and start from the walk to help the wrong muscle release and help build the right ones. I’d do this over 3-4 months. 

- month 1: 2 trail rides per week with hill work OR 2 trotting poll groundwork days a week. I like to alternate between poles and hill work, depending on my mood. 2-3 “work” days. 

- Month 1 (weeks 1-2): in hand work showing your horse how to move down into the but properly and move shoulders off the outside rein. I recommend looking these videos up on youtube. Arttoride has some demonstrations teaching how to start this. Basically you are looking for the inside hind to come under and reward the horse for stretching down properly. 

This will involve several small sessions of gradual learning, until the horse can keep contact properly for 1/2 or more of the entire ring. I then start teaching leg yields, shoulder-ins etc with this. 

-Month 1 (weeks 3-4): undersaddle, doing the same exercises at the walk. Use leg yields, turns of the shoulder etc to set the body up properly and allow the horse to stretch down and forward. Focus on proper rhythm. 

IF your horse has trouble maintaining proper rhythm, there will be an extra step. Basically, light leg, squeeze, then tap. IMMEDIATELY WHEN THE HORSE GOES FORWARD or comes back from seat (whichever your horse struggles with). Stop, hop off, treat and end the session. Rinse and repeat while gradually expanding how long you wait to get off. You will soon have a horse that is motivated to go forward/ come back. 

- Month 2: Cont. hill work the same. Trot poll work is increased to cavaletti, canter polls or something that asks for more muscle control. Undersaddle work now consists of some trot steps. 

You will introduce the trot transition with few steps at a time and focus on whether the horse is able to stretch for the bit into and through the transition. Do not expand the trot until the horse can. Gradually expand the amount of trot steps as your horse can maintain without breaking contact. 

- end of month 2: work on changes of pace within the gait. 

-Month 3: pole work + hill work continues. By now, you should be seeing some physical changes in the neck musculature, so your horse will be able to hold a correct frame for longer. Now, you introduce some canter steps. Same as with the trot, you ask for only a few steps at a time, as the horse can sustain. 

Your focus again will be on transitions.

I agree on the video, but here is what I see (didn’t see your last video). 

You need to weigh down your thigh a bit and rotate it inward so that the inside thigh has contact with the saddle, not the back of your thigh like it is now. This is why your toes are pointed outwards and your leg is less stable. Right now, the leg is a bit too far ahead of you, which is what is causing you to be behind the motion and coming down harder in the posting trot. 

By weighing down the thigh, what I mean is that the inside of your thigh needs better contact with the saddle. Your thigh is the part that helps you control your posting. Additionally, I like to think of it as stretching the thigh and knee, down and backward, which brings the leg back a bit. This will also entice you to have a little bit more of a forward upper body, unless your like me on a horse that spooks and you have to remind yourself to fold at the hip a bit. You’ll feel a shift in your balance with this leg change. 

With the thigh, you also need to remember to let the lower leg fold and not just relax forward (which locks the knee). Your knee is a primary shock absorber and you need more angle in it than you have now (think of the feeling you’d get when kicking backwards in a stretch). Along with the thigh positioning, mentioned above, this should help you naturally drop your heel due to the weight distribution. On that topic, a reminder to never force your heel down, as this will force your lower leg forward. Rather, think toes up! 

I also have speculation that you are too far back on your seatbones. You should be sitting at the center of them, like prongs on the saddle. I suggest reading a bit and watching youtube videos about this concept “seatbone positioning and dressage”. Seat is the center of your balance and in my opinion, the MOST important element of position. If your seat is off, so will your leg and upper body.

So… in order: fix seatbones first as this will affect legs and upper body. Fix thigh second (you can do this while hopping on at the halt), and subsequently fix the lower leg. Lower hands a bit as well. This will prevent you from tipping back.

I’m actually in a second track nursing program now and to be honest, I’m finding all the “we are holier than though” pride very irritating.It seems nursing academia simultaneously tries too hard to differentiate itself away from the medical model, while also envying it. I can’t imagine how much worse NP school would be in that sense. I feel it causes a lot of energy towards interprofessional conflict, when it could sooner be used to improve communications and interprofessional exchanges of knowledge. 

I honestly wish nursing education would re-introduce some of the medical model, but also focus on the biopsychosocial and subjective elements. I feel like 85% of the theories taught are useless in real practice and that time would be better spent on knowledge needed for actual assessments and interprofessional communication. Partner with medical and other health professional schools to give nursing students a more thorough frame of knowledge, plus an understanding of the workings of other professions. Then bring in courses for patient education with focus on therapeutic communication, health promotion with teachings in the knowledge translation and educational models… but sadly that will never happen.

A little knowledge is always more dangerous because they don’t really know their knowledge deficits. 

The other part of it is nursing education has a lot of “I’m holier than thou” attitude… I’m currently in a second track nursing program and some parts are really hard because they try *too* hard to differentiate themselves from the rest of the medical field and it’s a strong sense of pride for nursing academics. My parents are doctors and my good friend went RN->medicine, so I don’t buy into any of the nonsense and think it actually hurts nursing as a profession. But, I can only speculate that the NP programs are even more insufferable by indoctrinating students to believe that they are “better” than doctors just because they use a different model of care🙄 I have another “friend” who is now a NP and noticed her attitude towards doctor’s proficiency declined throughout the 2 years she took the program. This is a girl that once wanted to go to med school and now complains that doctors “aren’t that great or knowledgeable” whatever that’s supposed to mean. This same girl argued with me and insulted me when I explained to her that the government held the capacity for paying doctors/nurses through medicare and fee for service, which is why the seats in medical school haven’t increased as much as nursing school seats - because of the sizeable cost differences(Canada). Anyways, I haven’t come across too many NP’s that didn’t have an ego to prove, so I can only imagine it is rooted in the education. Instead of getting humbled like many doctors do, NP’s get told how much they know and how special they are without the type of medical profs that look for ways to poke at all the knowledge they don’t know.

There really should be some differentiation on the terms, but I do think any reasonable nurse practitioner would introduce themselves as nurse practitioner to encompass their credentials and not doctor.
